name: Bolivia
summary: A landlocked Andean republic named after Simón Bolívar, independent since 1825, with a large Indigenous population.

knownFor.label: Potosí silver
knownFor.note: The Cerro Rico mine made Potosí one of the richest colonial cities.

knownFor.label: Mi Teleférico
knownFor.note: The world’s largest urban cable-car network, in La Paz.

location.value: Central South America, landlocked; about 1,098,581 km².

terrain.value: The high Altiplano, the Andes, and eastern lowlands.

climate.value: Cold on the Altiplano, tropical in the lowlands.

resources.value: Silver, tin, natural gas, zinc and some of the world’s largest lithium reserves.

disasters.value: Droughts, floods and landslides, especially in the Altiplano and Amazon lowlands.

urbanisation.value: Santa Cruz is the largest city; La Paz–El Alto is a major urban centre.

disease.value: Chagas disease and malnutrition occur in rural areas, and altitude affects health in the Andes.

migration.value: Migration from the highlands to Santa Cruz and abroad.

economicBase.value: Mining, natural gas, farming (soya, quinoa) and small trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Exports pass through Chilean and Peruvian ports; Bolivia runs a free zone at Ilo, Peru.

wealth.value: A developing country; the second-poorest in South America.

moneyAndTax.value: The boliviano, introduced in 1987 after hyperinflation.

inequality.value: Historic inequality between elites and Indigenous people.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic; the 2009 constitution renamed it the Plurinational State of Bolivia.

keyRulers.value: Simón Bolívar and Antonio José de Sucre (founders). Víctor Paz Estenssoro. Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: Presidents have changed through elections and, in the 20th century, many coups.

stability.value: Many coups, and the 1952 revolution, which gave Indigenous people the vote and land reform.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalries between regions (Andean highlands and eastern lowlands) and between parties and unions.

armyAndTech.value: A small army with a history of intervening in politics.

majorWars.value: War of the Pacific (1879–83) and Chaco War (1932–35).

territoryChange.value: Lost its coast to Chile after the War of the Pacific (1883); lost Acre to Brazil (1903) and part of the Gran Chaco to Paraguay (1932–35).

alliancesRivals.value: Seeks sovereign access to the Pacific.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; Tiwanaku and Inca engineering are older achievements.

scienceEducation.value: San Francisco Xavier University in Sucre (1624).

openness.value: Varied: open to trade but wary of foreign control of natural resources.

communicationTransport.value: Cable cars (Mi Teleférico) carry commuters between La Paz and El Alto, opened in 2014; there are few railways.

languageWriting.value: Spanish, Quechua, Aymara, Guaraní and others.

artsArchitecture.value: Andean textiles and music; colonial baroque churches.

socialStructure.value: An Indigenous majority (including Quechua and Aymara) and a mestizo and European-descent minority.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Indigenous identity, recognised in the 2009 constitution of a “plurinational” state.

dailyLife.value: Adobe houses on the Altiplano; potatoes, quinoa, salteñas.

ideasReligions.value: Indigenous rights movements and the “plurinational” state shaped politics in the 2000s.

colonisation.value: A former Spanish colony known as Upper Peru, famous for the silver mines of Potosí.

peakPeriod.value: Gas revenues funded social programmes after the 2006 hydrocarbon nationalisation.

declineSignals.value: Loss of the coast to Chile after 1883; many coups in the 20th century.

outcome.value: Bolivia continues as an independent state.
